title: Chasing Alpha
scopeNote: This keeps the live alpha calculation from a correlation model and the three numbers that move together. The item pool, the choice of which item to paraphrase, the inter-item correlation matrix and both closing challenges stay in the longer version. One structural change: the scale here is a fixed ten items, so a duplicate displaces a question rather than being added to the end.
summary: A ten-item scale where you choose how many items are near-duplicates of one another. Alpha climbs past 0.94, the content narrows from five areas to one, and the correlation with the outcome falls by about a quarter.
learningObjectives: State what Cronbach's alpha is a function of.
Explain why near-duplicate items raise alpha efficiently.
Explain why raising alpha that way costs content coverage when scale length is fixed.
Explain why a high alpha is not evidence that a scale measures what it claims.
Distinguish internal consistency from unidimensionality and from validity.
Say what kind of evidence would be needed to tell a good scale from a repetitive one.
interactionTypes: a prediction about validity before the scale is opened
a live control over how many items are near-duplicates
alpha, criterion validity and content coverage recomputed together
two lines diverging across every version of the scale
a live statement of what the ten items now ask about
a guided setting that pushes alpha as high as it goes
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. No questionnaire is administered to the learner.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with scale composition on a native range input reporting its value in text. Every figure in the chart is also given as a readout tile and in the chart description, so the two lines are never the only route to the numbers, and each line is labelled by name at its end rather than distinguished by colour. A live sentence states in words what the ten items now ask about and how much of the score is wording variance. The vertical axis is labelled as starting at 0.3 rather than zero. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Fictional items and a fictional criterion. Every figure is the value a specified correlation model implies for a population, not an estimate from a sample, so nothing here carries sampling error or a confidence interval.
simulationNotes: Items are standardised and generated by a general factor, a content-area factor, a wording factor shared only by near-duplicates, and item-specific error. The correlation between two items is therefore the sum of the products of their shared loadings, and alpha follows from the total-score variance as (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - k / Var(T)). The criterion loads on the general factor and on breadth of content coverage, and not at all on wording, which is the asymmetry the whole demonstration rests on: a duplicate adds to Var(T), the denominator of the validity coefficient, without adding to its numerator. The structural change from the original is deliberate. In the full version items are appended, which raises alpha sharply but leaves validity nearly flat, because coverage is diluted rather than lost. Fixing the scale at ten items makes each duplicate cost a question, which is how construction works under a length budget, and the two lines then genuinely diverge: alpha 0.82 to 0.94, validity 0.62 to 0.46, coverage five areas to one. The duplicate's general loading is 0.54 against a distinct item's 0.55, deliberately close, because a near-duplicate is a perfectly good item on its own and its fault is redundancy rather than weakness. That also makes alpha rise monotonically, so no single step of the control shows alpha falling and invites the wrong conclusion from an artefact of the loadings. Simplifications: no sampling error; continuous standardised items, so no distinction between alpha, standardised alpha and ordinal alpha; and a single wording family.
readmeTopic: why a high Cronbach's alpha is not evidence that a scale is any good
